# TO THE READER

utterly contrary to this excellent **matter** <term>Matter (materia): in alchemy, this refers to the "Prima Materia" or the raw starting material required to begin the Great Work.</term>, having commanded them all to **go to the crows** <note>original: "ἐς κόρακας" (es korakas); a Greek idiom meaning to be cast away or "be damned."</note>. ...since water for its **nourishment** <note>original: "alimoniam"; in alchemical theory, the "stone" is often treated as a living thing that must be fed or sustained with liquid, often called "mercurial water."</note>, a small vessel to contain it, a smaller **furnace** <term>Furnace: specifically a "furnellus," a small oven or athanor designed to maintain a steady, gentle heat over a long period.</term> to enclose it, and—so that its heat may be fostered—an **invisible fire** <term>Invisible Fire: "ignis invisibilis"; a central alchemical concept referring to a natural or chemical heat that does not produce a visible flame, often identified with the internal energy of the "Philosophical Mercury" or the heat of fermentation.</term> are all required; nevertheless, because a longer time is necessary—at least a span of two years—excessive activity and haste toward the end could cause you to lose everything. # JEAN HÉROARD.

Behold, Lagneus himself dedicates to you his *Harmony*, <note>original: "Harmoniam". The letters of your name, when rearranged, add a spur to one already running and wings to one who flies. Wondrously rushing toward bright honors by the gift of the gods,
Along a direct and lawful path.
A path flourishing with the honor of a flower toward the power of the excellent,
Helping heroes with a more noble nard. <note>term: nard (spikenard), a costly aromatic ointment used in antiquity as a symbol of high honor or burial rite.</note>
Live, renowned hero, steadfastly adorning the Muses; <note>The Muses were the nine Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note>
Say: "I am carried to the stars, forever renewing them by my new art"—
The stars that radiate most brightly in our sky,
The stars that wear the crown of the French.

*Jean Fernel.* <note>original: "Ioannes Fernelius." A prominent French physician who sought to reconcile traditional medicine with chemical observations.</note>

*John Isaac Hollandus.* <note>original: "Ioannes Isaacus Hollandus." One of the "Hollandi," a pair of father-and-son alchemists from the Netherlands whose work influenced Paracelsus.</note>
*John Pontanus.* <note>original: "Ioannes Pontanus." Known for his "Epistle on the Philosophical Fire," where he claims to have found the secret of the Great Work after many failures.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the alphabetical index of authors (concluding with Vincent of Beauvais) into a series of philosophical and practical justifications for the study of alchemy. It is necessary to bring forward many arguments against strongly held opinions if one wishes to lead a listener away from their previous view and convert them so they might have faith in one’s words. Indeed, I would not have produced these things for the confirmation of my speech if there were not so many people who opposed my opinion. <note>original: "Hippocrates lib. 4. de morbis, sect. 15." Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) was the most famous physician of antiquity. Alchemists frequently cited him to provide a "medical" and authoritative foundation for their theories.</note>

Every thing which is bought at a high price is a lie. <note>original: "Morienes in Aurora Cons. pag. 217." Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit; the *Aurora Consurgens* (The Rising Dawn) is a famous 15-century illuminated manuscript often attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note>

The expenses of our <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" or "Great Work" (Ars) is the standard term used by practitioners to describe the process of alchemical transformation.</note> do not exceed the price of two gold coins in its first purchase. <note>original: "Anonymus apud Theob." Citing an anonymous author found in the works of Theobald of Hoghelande, who was mentioned on the previous page.</note>

You should hold this firmly: that for all the chapters of this most precious art, the price of the medicines themselves does not exceed the expenditure of fifty silver pieces, calculating from the first operation. <note>original: "Arnaldus, Rosarij lib. 2. cap. 7." Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311) was a celebrated physician and religious reformer; the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers) is one of the most influential texts in the alchemical tradition.</note>

Whatever exceeds the value of one ounce of gold is not according to the intention of the higher order. <note>original: "Propositiones Artis Chemicæ, Propos. 12." This refers to a set of standardized "Propositions of the Chemical Art" used as axioms by practitioners.</note>

# DAVID LAGNEUS

...that the matter is a **worthless thing** <note>original: "rem vilem." Alchemists frequently claimed that the "First Matter" of their work was a common substance found everywhere, often overlooked or despised by the ignorant.</note>. And when they had sublimated it, they called it a **serpent**, and a **poisonous beast**. And when they had calcined the same, they said it was **salt**, and things of this sort. When they had dissolved it, they called it **water**, and said it was found in all places. And when they had brought the matter to the state of oil, they called it a **viscous thing** and **commonly for sale**. But when they had congealed it, they named it **earth**, and said that the poor as well as the rich possess it. And when they had drawn out its whiteness <note>This refers to the *Albedo* or "whitening" stage, a major milestone in the Great Work signifying purification.</note>, they called it **virgin’s milk** and **something white**. And when they had sublimated its redness upwards, they called it **fire** and **something red** <note>This refers to the *Rubedo* or "reddening" stage, the final stage of the process where the Stone achieves its full power.</note>. And in this way, according to how the matter of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> was turned into a peculiar nature, they gave it a name, until it was brought to the end.

John Isaac Hollandus <note>A reference to the Dutch alchemist whose work provides the basis for this description of the Stone's changing names.</note>

<summary>This page explains how the names of the alchemical substance change according to its chemical state—such as "serpent" when volatile, "salt" when calcined, and "virgin's milk" when white. It highlights the alchemical tradition of using metaphors to describe the shifting physical properties of the "Stone" during its creation.</summary>

# Chemical Harmony

Book 1 of *Mineral Works*, chapter 126.

<margin>Greuer</margin>
After the materials have been amalgamated <note>To "amalgamate" usually meant to combine mercury with another metal, but in a philosophical sense, it refers to the union of the two primary principles of the Work.</note>, this amalgam—in order to hide it from the unworthy <note>Alchemists were notoriously secretive, believing their knowledge should only be revealed to those with pure intentions, rather than those seeking literal gold out of greed.</note>—is usually called by the Philosophers **our bronze**, **our gold**, **earth of magnesia** <note>original: "terra magnesia." In alchemy, "magnesia" does not refer to the modern element magnesium, but to a mysterious, dark "prime matter" that contains the potential for the Stone.</note>, and **the whole composite**. This **Blackness** <note>Known as the *Nigredo* stage, the first major phase of the "Great Work," representing the death or decay of the old matter before it can be reborn.</note> receives a thousand names. For it is called **fire**, **soul**, **cloud**, and the **raven’s head** <note>original: "caput corvi." Alanus <note>Likely Alanus ab Insulis, a medieval scholar to whom several alchemical treatises were attributed.</note>, page 56.

For it is **watery**, **airy**, **fiery**, **earthy**, **phlegmatic**, **choleric**, **me-** <note>The text likely cuts off here before finishing the word "melancholic," which would complete the list of the four "humors" or temperaments that correspond to the four elements.</note>

# Chemical Harmony.

A iij <note>A signature mark used by printers to help bind the book's pages in the correct order.</note>

<margin>Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated medieval physician and alchemist whose works emphasize the unity of the three realms of nature in the alchemical process.</note></margin>This composition made from three [parts] is called the *Blessed Stone*, mineral, animal, and vegetable, because it has no proper name of its own. It is *Mineral*, because it is composed of minerals. It is *Vegetable*, because it comes to life and grows <note>original: "viuifcit & crescit." In alchemical theory, the "vegetation" of the stone refers to its ability to multiply its power like a living plant.</note>. It is *Animal*, because it has a soul, a spirit, and a body, just like living animals. By another name it is called the **stinking blackness** <note>original: "nigrum fœtens." This refers to the *nigredo* or "blackening" stage, where the matter is said to putrefy, often accompanied by a foul odor, as its old forms are destroyed.</note>: because it has a black belly. It is also called *chaos, or the origin of the world, or a confused mass*: but we call it earth. And our water is called by the names of all leaves, trees, and greenery, so that they <note>The "Philosophers" or alchemists who wrote these texts to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note> might deceive the foolish. It is also called *blessed water, the moderation of the wise, the sharpest vinegar <note>original: "acetum acerrimũ." This is a technical term for a powerful acid or solvent used to dissolve the base metal.</note>, the body that is dissolved, the gum of the Philosophers <note>original: "gumma Philosophorum." This describes the viscous, resin-like state the matter takes during heating.</note>, the cheap thing, the dear thing, the hard and opaque body, the soft and clear body, the exaltation of the water, and the cornerstone of the work <note>original: "angulus operis."</note>.*

...you will immediately find **blackness** <note>original: *nigredo*. <margin>Exercise on the *Assembly*.</margin>
**Mercury** is called, at the beginning of the work, **water**; then, when the blackness appears, it is called **earth**; next, when it has been sublimated <note>A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid, used here to represent purification.</note>, it is called **air**; then, when it has been reddened (for the "air" must be cooked by itself until it turns red), it is called **fire**. After this, when it is sublimated with some "luminous body" <note>original: *corpore luminari*. This usually refers to the "perfect" metals, gold (the Sun) or silver (the Moon).</note>, it is called **leaven** <note>original: *fermentum*. In alchemy, a substance that "ripens" or transforms the rest of the mixture, much like yeast in bread.</note>; finally, when it is added alone to the whole and composed matter, it is called **spirit**. And thus, the earth combined with water, air, and fire constitutes the "body"; the leaven is the "soul" or the final watering; and the spirit belongs to Mercury alone. — Exercise 9 on the *Assembly*.

<margin>*The Rising Dawn*.</margin>
Whoever desires to know many names and the reasons for them should see and read the book entitled *The Rising Dawn* <note>original: *Aurora consurgens*. A famous medieval alchemical treatise, often richly illustrated, that uses intense biblical and erotic metaphors to describe the chemical process.</note>.

<margin>Assembly of the Philosophers <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among ancient sages</note></margin>
Unless you grind, destroy, soak, and diligently govern the body until you extract its *fatness* <note>original: *pinguedinem*; in alchemy, this refers to the oily, combustible essence or "sulfur" within a substance</note> and create a *fine, impalpable spirit*, you labor in vain. # David Lagneau

When we make mention of *sublimation* <term>the process of heating a substance to transform it into vapor, thereby purifying it</term>, or even when we *sublimate*, we mean to separate that part which is above from that which is below. For in our *sublimation*, the fixed <term>stable and heat-resistant</term> parts are not raised, but only the parts that are not fixed. Alanus, page 49.

*Decoction <note>boiling or heating in a liquid</note>, mixing, sublimation, grinding, drying, watering, firing, whitening, and reddening*, and by whatever other names it may be called, it is nonetheless only one single regimen <term>a systematic method or procedure</term>, which grinding and decoction can rightly achieve. The same author, p. 55.

Our beginning, with body and spirit already joined, when it is united in the work, is called *calcination* <term>the reduction of a substance to a powder or ash through intense heat</term>. The same author, page 56.

Every thing is destroyed by the same cause through which it grows; nor is anything more agreeable to Nature than

## Chemical Harmony

<margin>Ventura <note>Laurentius Ventura was a 16th-century Venetian physician and alchemist, best known for his work *On the Method of Composing the Philosophical Stone*.</note></margin>
*Let the fire be gentle and even, so that it neither grows too strong nor becomes too weak.* Ventura, chapter 20.

<margin>The Rosary <note>original: "Rosarium"; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a highly influential 16th-century alchemical text featuring symbolic woodcuts.</note></margin>
Mercury is fire. Hence the Philosopher <note>A common title in alchemical texts for an ultimate authority, often Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle.</note> says: *Know therefore that Mercury is a fire burning bodies more than fire itself.* <note>original: "Mercurius est ignis corpora comburens magis quam ignis." # David Lagneus
### iii M

...does not wither nor is it consumed. <margin>The Rosary</margin> The same author, page 179.

Only *temperate heat* thickens moisture and perfects the mixture without being excessive. For the generations and procreations of natural things can only occur through a *most temperate and equal heat*, such as horse manure <note>original: "fimus equinus"; a common alchemical method for providing steady, gentle heat by burying a vessel in fermenting dung to act as a natural incubator.</note>, which is moist and warm. The same author, page 181.

In dissolution <term>solutio: the process of turning a solid into a liquid state</term>, the *fire shall always be light*; in sublimation <term>sublimatio: the process of vaporizing a solid to purify it, then collecting the crystals</term>, *moderate*; in coagulation <term>coagulatio: the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid</term>, *temperate*; in whitening <term>dealbatio: the stage of purification also known as the albedo</term>, *continuous*; in reddening <term>rubificatione: the final stage of the work, known as the rubedo</term>, *strong*. But if you err in these things through ignorance, you will very often weep over your failure and wasted labor. The same author, page 186.

Let the measure of the fire be the heat of the July Sun, so that through a gentle and long cooking <note>original: "decoctione"</note>, the water may be thickened and become black earth <note>original: "terra nigra"; this refers to the *nigredo* stage, the first phase of the Great Work characterized by putrefaction and the color black.</note>. The same author, page 201.

# Chemical Harmony.

### The Method of fermenting the physical Stone.

### GREETINGS TO THE READER.

*Since that passage by Fernel—from Book 2, Chapter 18 of **On the Hidden Causes of Things** <note>original: "de Abditis rerum causis." This was a highly influential work by Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a French physician who sought to integrate Platonic philosophy with medicine.</note>, regarding the extraction of the seed of gold—provided the primary inspiration for compiling this **Harmony** <note>The "Harmony" refers to the title of the book, "Harmonia Chemica," suggesting a reconciliation of different alchemical theories.</note>, it seemed to me that it would not be out of place to transcribe it here in its entirety. Furthermore, lest a few pages elsewhere remain blank, I have added one or two riddles. I hope you will receive this kindly. Farewell.*

<margin>Fernel</margin>The Philosopher’s Stone—called the **Elixir** by the Arabs—is the true seed for generating and propagating gold. It must be sought and tracked down not from sulfur, nor from mercury <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver." Sulfur and mercury were traditionally considered the two primary components of all metals in alchemical theory.</note>, nor from any of those other substances which many propose with much deceit, but from gold alone, and indeed from the purest gold.

...they may frequently thin themselves out and return most pure from all filth and dregs, having attained the highest powers. These two are the primary principles of the entire art and the work to be completed, in which the four elements of the world are bound together. For in the water, air is also present; in the calx, earth and fire; and so it is as we read in the **Emerald Tablet of Hermes**, <term>Smaragdine Tablet</term> <note>The *Tabula Smaragdina*, a foundational Hermetic text said to contain the secret of the "one substance" or the Philosopher's Stone.</note> as if it were a mystery carved in stone:

*It ascends from the earth into heaven, and again it descends into the earth, and thus it receives the power of the higher and lower things.* <note>original: "Ascendit a terra in coelum..." This famous maxim describes the circulation of the alchemical spirit (distillation and condensation) as a mirror of cosmic processes.</note>

Those who composed these things in riddles call this water **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term>, and the calx **true sulfur**. Through the mixing of these, the **Stone** is made, just as bread is made from water and flour. Others called the water the **living spirit** and the earth the **leaven** <term>fermentum</term> <note>Just as yeast transforms dough, the "leaven" or "ferment" was thought to transform the "body" of the metal into the Stone.</note>; others called the former the **sea** and the latter the **woman**, from whose embrace and union the **infant** <note>The "infant" or "child" is a common alchemical metaphor for the finished Stone, produced by the marriage of the King (Sulfur/Sun) and Queen (Mercury/Moon).</note> is brought forth. The final work, however...

...the infant, so that you may complete the work, bury the pure **calx** <term>calx</term> <note>original: "calcem" — A fine powder or residue resulting from the roasting of a metal; the "body" of the substance once its impurities have been removed.</note> in a sealed vessel and hide it away in warm **horse dung** <term>equino fimo</term> <note>Horse manure was a staple of the early laboratory, used as a natural, steady heat source for long-term "digestion" or incubation of chemical mixtures.</note> for forty days, until it liquefies into a white and thick liquid. Into this, at the proper intervals of days, gradually pour water: do so in the way and according to the method which the masters of the art have explained so perfectly, so that the **calx**, gradually drinking in all its water as if nourished by it, may thicken into a **true stone**.

The various changes of colors that the stone must undergo during this period of time, and the signs that indicate its finished and perfect state, have also been clearly expressed and revealed by those masters. This is the **immense treasure**, this the **true elixir** <term>elixir</term>, this the **fruitful seed of gold** <term>auri semen</term>. If one **drachma** <term>drachma</term> <note>A small unit of weight; the author is emphasizing the incredible potency of the finished Stone.</note> of this substance is poured into two hundred and fifty drachmas of molten **lead** <term>plumbum</term> or **tin** <term>stannum</term>, it will convert the entirety into the **purest gold** <term>aurum</term>.

# A CERTAIN ENIGMATIC
### EPITAPH
### Inscribed on a marble stone many centuries ago at Bologna, the city of studies. <note>Bologna was home to one of the oldest universities in Europe and was a major center for legal and scientific study.</note>

AELIA LAELIA CRISPIS <note>This name is a famous historical mystery. Scholars have debated for centuries whether she was a real person, a symbol for the soul, or—as the alchemists believed—a representation of the Materia Prima.</note>, NEITHER MAN NOR WOMAN, NOR HERMAPHRODITE <term>androgyna</term>, NOR GIRL, NOR YOUTH, NOR OLD WOMAN, NOR HARLOT, NOR CHASTE WOMAN, BUT ALL OF THESE.
TAKEN AWAY NEITHER BY HUNGER, NOR BY THE SWORD <note>original: "ferro" — literally "iron," commonly used to mean a blade or sword.</note>, NOR BY POISON: BUT BY ALL OF THEM.
SHE LIES NEITHER IN THE SKY, NOR IN THE WATERS, NOR IN THE LANDS, BUT EVERYWHERE.
LUCIUS AGATHO PRISCIVS, NEITHER HUSBAND, NOR LOVER, NOR KINSMAN <note>original: "necessarius" — a person bound by social or familial duty.</note>, NEITHER MOURNING, NOR REJOICING, NOR WEEPING, KNOWS AND KNOWS NOT WHAT HE HAS SET UP FOR WHOM: NEITHER THIS MASSIVE STRUCTURE <note>original: "molem"</note>, NOR PYRAMID, NOR TOMB, BUT ALL.
THIS IS A TOMB, HAVING NO CORPSE WITHIN;
THIS IS A CORPSE, HAVING NO TOMB WITHOUT;
BUT THE CORPSE IS THE SAME AS THE TOMB UNTO ITSELF.

<summary>This page records the famous "Aelia Laelia Crispis" riddle, a paradoxical Latin epitaph from Bologna. In an alchemical context, it serves as a poetic description of the elusive and contradictory nature of the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>
<keywords>Aelia Laelia Crispis, Bologna riddle, Lucius Agatho Priscius, paradox, epitaph, Materia Prima, alchemy, tomb allegory</keywords>

# THE SECRET OF THE
### PHILOSOPHERS, formerly composed in hexameter <term>hexametro</term> verse by a most learned man. <note>Hexameter is a classic form of rhythmic poetry most famous for its use in Greek and Roman epics like the works of Homer and Virgil.</note>

->In the name of the living and life-giving God.<-

->I.<-

Earth is my body, fire has provided me strength,
<margin><unclear>Earth</unclear></margin> I seek a high home, yet my seat is always in the depths:
And a moisture <note>original: "humor" — in alchemy, this refers to the "liquid" or "watery" state of a substance during transformation.</note> bathes me which quickly leaves me.

->II.<-

I have tears, indeed I have them, but there is no cause of sorrow,
There is a path to the heavens, but the heavy air hinders me:
And he who fathered me is not himself born without me. <note>This paradox describes the circular nature of the "Great Work," where the final product is often required to "seed" or complete the earlier stages.</note>

->III.<-

A thin dust of water, fallen with a modest weight,
Moist in the sun, flowing in summer, dry in the cold,
About to create rivers, I first occupy all the lands.

->IV.<-

I shall relate to you the wondrous origins <term>primordia</term> of our life:
I was not yet born, nor was I then in my mother’s womb,

<vocab>The Secret of the Philosophers, hexameter, Earth, fire, moisture, air, origins of life</vocab>

<summary>This page contains a series of four alchemical riddles written in Latin verse, personifying the Philosopher's Stone or the First Matter. Each stanza uses elemental paradoxes—such as "dry water" or a "son" who creates his own "father"—to describe the substance's transformative properties.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, Materia Prima, elemental riddles, hexameter verse, four elements, paradoxical nature</keywords>

--- Page 374 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Secret of the Philosophers," a series of alchemical riddles written in verse. The previous page (124) ended mid-riddle with the narrator describing their existence before being in their mother's womb. This page completes that thought and presents five further riddles (V through IX) exploring themes of life, death, and the transformation of matter.</meta>

<page-num>325</page-num>
<sig>X iij</sig>

*Now that the birth is over, no one saw me born.* <note>This line concludes Riddle IV from the previous page, emphasizing the invisible or "occult" nature of the alchemical birth.</note>

->V.<-

*I cannot be born, if I do not kill my mother:*
*I killed my mother, but the same end awaits me.*
*My death suffers the same thing that my origin <term>origo</term> already did.* <note>In alchemy, the "mother" often refers to the base matter or the chemical matrix which must be destroyed or dissolved for the new substance to arise.</note>

->V I.<-

*Life for me is death, I die if I begin to be born:*
*But the fate of death <note>original: "fatum lethi"</note> comes before the beginning of light:*
*Thus I consider the spirits of the dead <term>manes</term> alone to be my parents.* <note>The "manes" were the ancestral spirits of the Roman underworld. Here, the author suggests the substance is born from "dead" or putrefied matter.</note>

->V I I.<-

*I am not great indeed, but the greatest power <term>virtus</term> is in me,*
*The spirit is great, although in a small body,*
*Neither does my seed hold harm, nor does my fault bring a blush.*

->V I I I.<-

*We are both stones, we are one, we both lie down:*
*As sluggish as one is, so much the other is not slow;*
*This one remains unmoved, that one does not cease to move.* <note>This describes the union of the "Fixed" (stable/immobile) and the "Volatile" (active/moving) principles in alchemy.</note>

->I X.<-

*No one is able to split me, though many can cut me down.*
*But I am many-colored <term>versicolor</term>, destined to be white at some time.*
*I prefer to remain black; I will fear my final fate less.* <note>This refers to the stages of the alchemical "Great Work": the black stage (*Nigredo*) and the white stage (*Albedo*). To "cut down" without "splitting" implies a change in form without a loss of essential unity.</note>

<vocab>birth, death, origin, life, fate, spirits of the dead, power/virtue, spirit, stones, many-colored</vocab>

<summary>This page presents five paradoxical riddles (V–IX) that personify the alchemical substance through themes of matricide, rebirth from death, and the union of opposites. These verses describe the transition of the "Stone" from the black, putrefied stage toward the white stage of purification.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, paradox, Nigredo, Albedo, fixed and volatile, personification, philosophical death, First Matter</keywords>

### X.

I have no fixed shape <term>figura</term>, nor is any shape foreign to me. <note>This likely refers to a mirror or perhaps Mercury, which takes the shape of its container and reflects all things.</note>
A brightness <term>fulgor</term> dwells within, gleaming with radiant light,
Which reveals nothing, unless it has seen something before.

### XI.

I do not die straight away while my spirit <term>spiritus</term> departs. <note>original: "spiritus exit"</note>
For it returns constantly, although it also often recedes:
And to me now the soul <term>anima</term> is a great power <term>facultas</term>, and now it is nothing. <note>This riddle describes the alchemical process of distillation or "circulation," where vapors (the spirit) rise and fall within a sealed vessel, repeatedly "leaving" and "returning" to the matter.</note>

### XII.

I have endured more than one body <term>corpus</term> ought to.
I had three souls, all of which I held within.
<margin>The greatest difficulty.</margin>
Two have departed, but the third has almost followed. <note>The "three souls" are likely the three alchemical principles: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt. The departure of two suggests a stage of purification where only the final essence remains.</note>

---

There is no clearer way to deny than by saying, "No."
And there is no clearer way to affirm than by saying, "Yes." <note>original: "Ita"</note>
To whom it has not been given, he does not understand. For every gift <term>donum</term> is from above. <note>This reflects the common alchemical belief that the "Great Work" cannot be accomplished by labor alone, but requires divine grace or "donum Dei."</note>

---

You will seek much and you will not find,
Perhaps you will find when you do not seek.

☛ Page 4, line 1: read **melancholic** <note>original: "melancholicus." In the theory of the four humors, this relates to the "black bile," often associated in alchemy with the first stage of the work, the *nigredo* or blackening.</note>. Page 36, [line] 4: **stone, red**, read **red stone** without the punctuation <note>original: "abſque diſtinctione." The author is correcting a comma that incorrectly separated the noun from its adjective.</note>. Page 34, [line] 3: in the margin, read **Hoghelande** <note>Theobald van Hoghelande (c. 1560–1608) was a significant Dutch alchemist who wrote defenses of the art against skeptics.</note>. Page 43, [line] 10: read **almagra** <note>*Almagra* is a term of Arabic origin referring to red ochre or red earth, often used as a synonym for the "red sulfur" or the final stage of the Alchemical Stone.</note>. Page 115, [line] 21: after **coagulation**, add **calcination** <note>original: "coagulatio" and "calcinatio." Calcination is the process of reducing a solid to powder through high heat, while coagulation is the thickening of a liquid into a solid.</note>. Page 141, [line] 22: read **with salt and vinegar**. Page 268, [line] 3: in the margin, read **Valescus** <note>Likely Valescus de Taranta (c. 1360–1418), a renowned medieval physician whose works were frequently cited in medical and alchemical texts.</note>.
